skyline.text: Why Amit Varma obeys the law but calls no government legitimate
Ajay Shah recalls a verdict on a finance minister’s advisers
How norms kept him from becoming one more dictator

brief.head: Legal, not legitimate
brief.text: Stalin’s Russia ran on laws, Ajay Shah said, yet everybody hated the regime. The NKVD had the legal authority to grab you from your bedroom. {098-C03}

brief.head: Brain without fingers
brief.text: Lant Pritchett’s paper calls India a flailing state: a brilliant brain of senior officials, nerves to the fingers severed. Cynical functionaries, Shah said, are one cause. {098-R05}

brief.head: The passport test
brief.text: Weber’s legal-bureaucratic legitimacy, Shah said, looks like a passport office with a known procedure: 14 accepted kinds of identity, show any three, no friend in government needed. {098-J15}

brief.head: Loved until the fall
brief.text: Under an illegitimate regime the people clap and the media praises. Everybody in East Germany loved the Communist Party, Shah said, until the day it fell, friendless. {098-J10}

brief.head: The knife stays sharp
brief.text: Even an ideologue with a cultural programme needs legitimacy, Shah argued. A legitimate authority can move people 10 per cent its way and slowly shift social norms. {#tenpercent}

thought.text: You need a very soft currency called respect.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, advising every leadership, of states and companies alike

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on political legitimacy
lead.head: A monopoly is not a mandate
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah sat in the summer sun to discuss a subject that, Varma said, is like the sun: “It is ubiquitous. We experience it every day, and yet we kind of take it for granted, which is the Indian state.” {098-J01}
Shah widened the brief at once. Not just the Indian state, he said: the subject was of great interest to viewers “ranging from Germany to Mozambique”.
He began with Max Weber, who defined the state as the community that achieves and maintains a monopoly of violence in a given territory. The episode was about the partner of that idea: legitimacy.

Legitimacy, Shah said, is the belief of the people that the state has a right to rule over them. Where it exists, people give the state the benefit of the doubt, and its laws readily turn into social norms. {#define}
Where it is missing, the state must reach into every home by force. “Legitimacy matters because if all you have is coercive power, then you actually have very little,” he said. {098-C01}

Nor is it only a matter for citizens. Soldiers, policemen and civil servants must believe in the state too, Shah said, or they roll their eyes at each new edict and the ability to implement anything fades away. {098-C02}
## Where it comes from
Weber, Shah said, named three sources: tradition, the charisma of a great leader, and legal, bureaucratic procedure under the rule of law. Later scholars added a fourth, performance. {098-C04}
The hosts were recording in rural Maharashtra, where, Shah said, there had been twelve hours of power cuts a day for several days. “That’s not a path to state legitimacy.” {#powercuts}
## What it costs

Without legitimacy, Shah argued, much goes wrong. Spending on policing and surveillance balloons, interpersonal violence rises, people start lying to the state, talent and capital leave, and small problems snowball into big ones. {098-C06}

Even a ruler who cares only for himself should want legitimacy, he said, because coercion is costly and a legitimate government collects more tax. In India, he said, people “move entire industries into cash activities in order to avoid the GST”. {#cash}
A smart ruler, in other words, cultivates legitimacy in order to extract more, not less. {098-C07}

Shah, admitting that at 59 his memory was starting to fade, then read from notes a checklist for any politician or civil servant: transparency, accountability, procedural fairness, consultation, decentralisation, performance, visible expertise, respect for norms and telling the truth. {098-J03}
## Varma’s four thoughts

Then it was Varma’s turn. Compliance, or the absence of dissent, should not be mistaken for legitimacy, he warned. He himself considers no government legitimate, just as he rejects the social contract, since he never signed one. {098-C11}

Most Indians, he argued, thrive despite a parasitic state and are apathetic about its legitimacy, because power and accountability have come apart. Voting, he said, has become tribal loyalty, like supporting Manchester United or Liverpool. {098-J14}

The Constitution, Varma said, was more liberal than the society it governed. {098-C13} Politics has since caught up with society, and an English-speaking elite, he argued, cannot declare a government illegitimate just because it dislikes its values.
The real fight, he said, is in the marketplace of ideas, and that needs freedom. “Legitimacy is impossible without freedom.” {098-C14}
He allowed that he was perhaps casting a cynical eye on the whole episode. It was still important, he said, to look at all these frameworks of legitimacy and to aspire towards a better world.
lead.reelLabel: Hear the case in six parts

second.label: Roving and stationary
second.head: A bandit with prospects
second.deck: Mancur Olson’s bandits show why even a selfish ruler wants legitimacy
body: Amit Varma reached for two terms coined by the economist Mancur Olson. A roving bandit destroys a village completely, because he comes and goes. A stationary bandit intends to stay and keep robbing, so he has to let the people prosper. {098-R06}
Perversely enough, Varma said, this is public choice logic at work: even a bandit should at least try to be a legitimate one. {098-C08}

Ajay Shah carried the idea further. Under a bandit with legitimacy, villagers improve their land, start shops and businesses and build better homes. If the bandit robs and pillages as he likes, the people are more likely to just dig holes in the ground and hide their gold. {#gold}

quote.text: Even if you’re a bandit, it is in your interest to at least try to be a legitimate bandit.

second.caption: Mancur Olson’s two bandits

third.head: Howzat for legitimacy?
body: A lot of people see politics as a game, Ajay Shah said, and the media breathlessly reports election results as it would a cricket match.
But elections now happen in many countries. Vladimir Putin holds them, he pointed out, and wins with 85 per cent of the vote share. {#putin}
Populist regimes that pursue only their base, he said, can keep winning and still face a gap in legitimacy. Nor do 320 seats make a government fully legitimate, whatever the media shouts. {#seats}

Legitimacy lies inside people’s minds: “You have to go into the eye rolling of the civil servant or the citizen when one more fatwa comes from high above. That’s legitimacy, and you don’t get that merely by winning elections.” {098-C05}
third.caption: elections as cricket matches

p2.title: The right to rule
p2.deck: Ajay Shah builds the idea of legitimacy from Max Weber up; Amit Varma asks whether it matters in India

sections.label: The idea
sections.head: Believed, not merely obeyed
sections.caption: what legitimacy means
body: Amit Varma began with definitions, since a word can carry one meaning in everyday parlance and a more fixed one in political science. Ajay Shah’s answer: legitimacy is the belief of the people that the state has a right to rule over them. {#define}

It is “a very messy, soft construct”, he said. Told to drive on the left side of the road, a citizen of a legitimate state assumes there is probably some merit to it, and the rule becomes a convention.

Even an odd edict, such as wearing blue caps on Tuesday, is more likely to be followed where there is respect. Without that good faith the state must live by force, and “you can’t live by violence every day”. {098-C01}
## Inside the machine

In an illegitimate state, Shah said, a policeman reads each new clause in the IPC as a chance for a new protection racket. Handed a UIDAI-backed system for the PDS, a civil servant giggles inside and tells his buddies how to bypass it.
The functionaries of the state have to believe in its shared mission, virtue and competence, he said; otherwise the ability to implement anything fades away. {098-C02}

~ Nor is power the same thing. Varma called this the gap between political authority and political legitimacy. Once the state can break down any door without facing machine-gun return fire, Shah said, Weber’s first level is assured. “Then what?”

quote.text: So state legitimacy is not just about the eyes of the populace, it is also in the eyes of the state.

sections.label: The four sources
sections.head: Four roads to respect
sections.caption: where legitimacy comes from
body: Max Weber, Ajay Shah said, taught three directions from which legitimacy arises. The first is tradition. When Aurangzeb became emperor, he received the respect that had been given to the Mughal Empire for hundreds of years. Patriarchy gets a certain respect for free, because it has always been there.

The second is charisma. Napoleon was not part of the traditional system, since the French Revolution had killed off France’s dynastic rule, yet he achieved legitimacy through the sheer power of his character.
In India, Shah said, the closest example is Nehru, whose authority was moral and intellectual, “not merely that I have the big stick”. {#moral}
When Shah twice compared the state to a company, Amit Varma scolded him on behalf of a good friend, one Dr Shah, who keeps telling him a country is not like a company.
## Rules and results

The third source is legal, bureaucratic procedure under the rule of law: rules that are thought through and considered fair, so that getting a passport means following a due process, not phoning a friend in government.

~ Later scholars added a fourth: performance. Keep the peace and make the police and courts work, Shah said, and you are on a path to legitimacy. China’s Communist Party earned respect by delivering a 10x of per capita GDP. {#tenx}

quote.text: That a state earns legitimacy by getting shit done.

sections.label: The cost
sections.head: What distrust costs a state
sections.caption: what breaks without legitimacy
body: Amit Varma put the hard case. An authoritarian who has achieved the monopoly of violence might ask why legitimacy should matter to him. Ajay Shah answered with a chain of harms.

First, coercion. The government pours money into its coercive organs and builds a surveillance state, which Shah called a deadweight loss. To watch everyone, he said, “you may end up with like one in every three citizens being a security apparatus member”. {#threecitizens}
Interpersonal violence rises too, and Shah counted violence by the police and the hangman as part of it. {098-C06}
## A state gone blind

Next, information. People cheerfully volunteer information to a legitimate state, Shah said; to an illegitimate one they lie. Its ability to see, in the sense of James C. Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*, goes down. {098-J09}

Brain drain and capital flight follow, because fewer people will tie their lives to a state they do not trust. And small sparks, such as a Jat agitation in Haryana, can grow big in unexpected ways when nobody gives the state the benefit of the doubt.
~ The end of the chain, Shah said, is “the whole enchilada”: the stability of the regime itself. A legitimate state reaches beyond its base to a wide spectrum of people.

quote.text: A good society is one where there are low levels of interpersonal violence.

sections.label: Public choice
sections.head: Selfish reasons to be liked
sections.caption: the selfish case for legitimacy
body: Public choice theory assumes that the people who run the state are self-interested actors who do not care what a good society is. So Ajay Shah set decency aside and argued from their own interest.

Coercion is expensive and painful, he said. A more legitimate government finds greater acceptance of its taxes. Under the GST, by contrast, whole industries have moved into cash as people do all they can to avoid it. {#cash}
Legitimacy also buys stability, and a brittle regime that lives by violence every day cannot extract more resources. A smart ruler, Shah concluded, would cultivate it. {098-C07}
## The ideologue’s calculation

Then Shah took a ruler who wants neither money nor arbitrary power, only to push a cultural or nationalist programme. Such a ruler still needs a state that works, and an illegitimate state is blunt: civil servants roll their eyes and only portray compliance. {098-C09}
A programme forced on people makes them hate it more every day, he said. Legitimacy, by contrast, grows the nation rather than shrinking it.
~ Amit Varma, in mock outrage, accused Shah of teaching demagogues to think rationally, and asked how any government might actually earn legitimacy.

quote.text: So an enlightened king, an enlightened state would want to extract more for herself, not less.

sections.label: The checklist
sections.head: Show your working, minister
sections.caption: a toolkit for earning legitimacy
body: This, Ajay Shah said, is where the episode goes from abstract ideas to action. He read his checklist for every civil servant and politician from notes. {098-J03}

Transparency comes first: expert committee reports, public debate, and draft laws shown before they are enacted. Then accountability: grievance redressal, audit and low corruption, so that no income tax officer or policeman can harm people at will.

Procedural fairness means laws known in advance and enforced equally, with a fair hearing before a neutral judge. Shah invented an obscure rule to show the alternative: “Did you know that on camera you cannot be consuming Diet Coke? It has to be Diet Pepsi.” {098-J04}

Consultation means open consultations and town halls, though not plebiscites. Decentralisation pushes the most power to cities, where people can see their sidewalks repaired. And performance counts: from 1991 to 2011, he said, the Indian state wore a halo because it delivered a 4x of GDP growth. {#gdp4x}
## No tablets of stone
Expertise must be visible. Edicts cannot simply come down from the top of a mountain like Moses’s Ten Commandments, Shah said: “that earns no respect.” {098-J06}
~ Respect for norms and telling the truth complete the list. Propaganda, he warned, is corrosive, because people discover that they are being lied to.

quote.text: That I may disagree with the outcome, but I want to see that you have the brains, you have the smarts.

sections.label: Amit’s dissent
sections.head: Obedient, but not convinced
sections.caption: why legitimacy may not matter in India
body: Amit Varma first warned against mistaking compliance, or the absence of dissent, for legitimacy. Then he zoomed out in four steps.

First, himself. He will never consider any government legitimate, he said, just as he rejects the social contract. “I have never agreed to sign a social contract.” He obeys the law to stay out of jail, for practical reasons, not ethical ones. {098-C11}
Second, society. For most Indians the rule of law does not exist, he said; they thrive despite the state, as the title of Gurcharan Das’s *India Grows at Night* says. {098-R07}
Power and accountability have come apart, he argued, because India lacks decentralisation: the people he votes for cannot change his life, and those who can do not need his vote. {098-C12}
## Topsoil and the battle of ideas

Third, history. The Constitution was more liberal than a society driven by caste, sexism and misogyny. Ambedkar, Varma said, spoke of villages as dens of ignorance and saw the Constitution as just a topsoil. {098-J13}
The missed task was to spread liberal values bottom-up. Now politics has caught up with society. “You and I are the fringe,” he told Ajay Shah.
~ Fourth, freedom. Legitimacy needs an open contest of ideas, he said, and there is no level playing field if you freeze the opposition’s bank accounts and stop them from campaigning. {#bankaccounts}

quote.text: Our constitution was a constitution created by an initially unelected liberal elite and imposed on an illiberal society.

portraits.hint: Indian jurist, chief architect of the Constitution

side.boxText: Max Weber defined the state as the community that achieves and maintains a monopoly of violence, and gave legitimacy as its partner idea. Ajay Shah’s one recommendation was Weber’s *Politics as a Vocation*, “one of the great books of the world”. {098-R01}

contQuote.text: The people I vote for don’t have power to change my life. And the people who have power to change my life don’t need my vote.

p3.title: Stories of the state
p3.deck: A put-down, a puzzle and a prime minister’s restraint

stories.start: I remember uh a funny moment in Indian history.
stories.end: So Teams, expertise, competence, these things earn legitimacy.
stories.caption: Jagdish Bhagwati’s put-down
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why governments need visible expertise
stories.head: Economists? Then I’m a dancer
body: Soon after Yashwant Sinha became Finance Minister, Ajay Shah recalled, he shared a conference panel with the economist Jagdish Bhagwati. {098-S01}
Bhagwati helpfully turned to the new minister with advice. Expertise really matters, he said: get the best people in the country into your government as your advisers.
Sinha named a couple of people who were with him and would take part in his ruling arrangement. Bhagwati’s reply became famous: “If they are economists, then I’m a Bharatanatyam dancer.” {#natyam}

Shah called it a funny moment in Indian history, but he told it as part of his checklist for earning legitimacy. Edicts need visible reasoning, he said, because people may disagree with an outcome but still want to see that a government has the brains. {098-C10}
~ Teams, expertise and competence, Shah said: these things earn legitimacy.
stories.why: A government earns legitimacy partly by visibly assembling competent teams. Citizens and experts judge it by whom it chooses to listen to, and advisers who are experts only in name drain its credibility.

stories.start: And uh this particular book, When All Else Fails, asks a very fascinating question
stories.end: So I don't want to take a position on this.
stories.caption: the policeman and the beggar
stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a thought experiment from Jason Brennan
stories.head: Same blow, different uniform
body: Amit Varma’s recommendation came with a puzzle. The book was the philosopher Jason Brennan’s *When All Else Fails: The Ethics of Resistance to State Injustice*, which the hosts’ mutual friend Abhinav Singh had urged him to read. {098-R02}
It poses a two-part thought experiment. You are walking down the street and some random man starts hitting a beggar. Your first instinct is to intervene.

Now make the man a policeman with a lathi. You stay away. It is, Varma said, “not just a question of authority, but also a question of legitimacy”: in a way, you are according legitimacy to the policeman because of his uniform. {098-S02}

~ Varma said he did not want to take a position. Brennan had been his guest on *The Seen and the Unseen* five or six years ago; Varma threw many counterfactuals at him and was blown away by the clarity of his thinking.
stories.why: Our instincts quietly grant the state’s agents a moral licence we would never give a private person. The uniform does ethical work in our heads, which shows legitimacy to be a belief people hold, not just a legal status.
stories.postscript: In that conversation, Brennan referred to a book by Michael Huemer that is just on state legitimacy. {#huemer}

stories.start: Okay, so think of Javar Al Nehru. There was plenty of stuff
stories.end: that are just not done, and that earns respect, that earns legitimacy
stories.caption: the dictator Nehru chose not to be
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on norms as a source of power
stories.head: The power Nehru left unused
body: Looking for India’s closest example of charismatic legitimacy, Ajay Shah chose Jawaharlal Nehru: a well-loved figure, respected all over India, who of course won elections, “but that’s the least of it”.
When Nehru said “guys, we should think about something”, people took him seriously. His authority, Shah said, was moral and intellectual. {#moral}

Later, Shah returned to Nehru to make a point about restraint. The Indian state was quite limited at the time, he said, and there was plenty Nehru could have done. “He could literally have gone down the path of becoming one more third world dictator.” He did not. {098-S03}

~ Norms, in Shah’s account, are an intangible path to charismatic power. Using hard power crudely, and destroying norms simply because one can, hinders legitimacy. People want to see a nice guy, he said, a graceful person.

quote.text: There was decency, there were norms, there were many things that are just not done, and that earns respect, that earns legitimacy.

quiz.q: What did Jagdish Bhagwati say he would be if the new finance minister’s advisers were economists?
quiz.a: A Bharatanatyam dancer, as he told Yashwant Sinha on a conference panel.

quiz.q: According to Max Weber, as Ajay Shah explained, what are the three sources of legitimacy?
quiz.a: Tradition, charisma, and legal, bureaucratic procedure under the rule of law.

quiz.q: Which leader did Ajay Shah cite to show that winning elections does not confer legitimacy?
quiz.a: Vladimir Putin, who holds elections and wins about 85 per cent of the vote.

quiz.q: In Mancur Olson’s terms, why does a stationary bandit let the village prosper?
quiz.a: Because he intends to stay and keep robbing, so something must be left.

quiz.q: Why does Amit Varma refuse to accept the social contract?
quiz.a: A contract needs voluntary consent between parties, and he never signed one.

quiz.q: In Jason Brennan’s thought experiment, what do most people do when a policeman beats a beggar?
quiz.a: They stay away, according the uniformed man a legitimacy they would deny a stranger.
